title: Omnia Browser
description: UI design and UX research for Omnia Browser, a spatial browser and media app for Vision Pro, Meta Quest and iOS, built over seven months at Omnia.
hmw: optimize spatial content discovery and distribution on emerging smart‑glasses platforms to empower AR creators to increase engagement, monetization, and growth?

blocks.text: Spatial Browser

Spatial photos, video and the web are locked inside proprietary ecosystems. Over seven months at Omnia, I was UI designer and UX researcher on a browser for Vision Pro, Meta Quest and iOS that opens them up.
Fifteen interviews and a competitor review

I conducted 15+ interviews with traditional media users, creators looking to publish spatial content, headset owners and company founders, who spoke to business use cases. I reviewed the media-sharing apps on Apple Vision Pro and Meta Quest, native and third-party, to find the gaps. I also coordinated with a full-stack team on development, backend and AI recommendations, and prototyped in Figma and then in code. With the team, I turned the findings into personas for viewers and creators and into affinity maps of pain points, core needs and prioritized features.
New ways to view content

Omnia lets people upload and explore Spatial Photos, Panoramas, Videos and Gaussian Splats, formats usually locked inside proprietary ecosystems. I designed a community-powered gallery for VR/AR headsets that turns spatial content into a shared, explorable space.
Articles, WebPages, Media ... and more!
Designed new interfaces to view AI summaries and full web pages with spatial media.

Flipping through summary cards is efficient, spatial and works alongside other apps. User research showed that people read more of the content AI summaries generate, and now they can do it in augmented reality.

On a page, all images sit in a top carousel for immediate access, followed by the text. Only the text in view is bright and the rest is dimmed to avoid visual distraction; scrolling brings the next text into view. The AI summaries are available in a side panel if you want them. Easy access to an AI assistant mattered for the future of browsing, so it lives in the Safari-inspired bottom tab bar.
These design elements predate Apple’s spatial web browsing update in visionOS 26.
Same web-based games… with spatial controls
WebXR games promise immersive play, but fragmentation across VR/AR devices has limited their reach.
Omnia makes spatial games cross-compatible with no developer intervention. I designed the Adaptable Game UI so interfaces morph to match the hardware in real time.
Picture gripping a virtual steering wheel rendered for your device, without a line of extra code. That is Omnia’s adaptive runtime.
Intuitive Zoom & Rotation Controls

I designed new zoom sliders and rotation controls for 3D models. They let users view and move a model with one hand, instead of the two-handed gestures native to the OS. Factory workers asked for this most, because of the nature of their work.
Buy what you see
I adapted the 3D model viewer for e-commerce. Users can see a product listing with its related videos, models and photos, plus the description, price and more.
Checkout uses Apple Pay, so users authenticate with the built-in Face ID without added steps.
Three calls that shaped the browser

cards.label: Dimmed reading layer
cards.value: Chose to dim all but the text in view, because it avoids visual distraction while reading in a headset.

cards.label: One-handed 3D controls
cards.value: Chose zoom sliders and rotation controls over the OS’s native two-handed gestures, because factory workers asked for one-handed use.

cards.label: Adaptive game UI
cards.value: Chose interfaces that morph to the hardware in real time over per-device work, because fragmentation across VR/AR devices had limited WebXR games.

blocks.text: Limits

items: There are no outcome metrics for Omnia Browser. What I can show is the research and the designs.
The one-handed 3D controls came from factory workers’ requests. I have no measured result for them.
The personas and affinity maps were shared work with the team, so the study says “we” for them.
